interactions.label: Why are schizonts of Plasmodium falciparum characteristically absent from the pe

params.question: Why are schizonts of Plasmodium falciparum characteristically absent from the peripheral blood smear?

answers.text: P. falciparum completes all schizogony within hepatocytes and never enters the erythrocytic cycle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: P. falciparum does undergo erythrocytic schizogony with a 48-hour cycle. Schizonts are absent from the peripheral smear because PfEMP1-mediated cytoadherence sequesters infected red blood cells in the deep microvasculature before they mature.

answers.text: Infected red blood cells expressing PfEMP1 adhere to vascular endothelium and are sequestered in the microvasculature

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PfEMP1 on knob-like surface projections binds endothelial receptors, trapping infected RBCs in capillaries of the brain and placenta. These cells never return to the peripheral circulation or the spleen, explaining the absence of schizonts on the blood film.

answers.text: The spleen rapidly destroys all schizont-containing red blood cells before they reach peripheral blood

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sequestered cells actually evade the spleen altogether. PfEMP1-mediated adhesion to vascular endothelium keeps infected RBCs trapped in the microvasculature, preventing splenic clearance — which is precisely how P. falciparum achieves high parasitaemia.

answers.text: Schizonts rupture too rapidly during the 48-hour cycle to be captured on a routine blood film

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The timing of rupture is not the issue. Schizonts are absent because PfEMP1-mediated cytoadherence sequesters infected red blood cells in the deep microvasculature, preventing them from circulating in peripheral blood.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key mechanism is PfEMP1-mediated sequestration. Infected red blood cells express PfEMP1 on knob-like projections, which binds vascular endothelium and traps them in cerebral and placental capillaries — this is why schizonts are absent from the peripheral blood film.
Well done. PfEMP1-mediated sequestration is the central mechanism that explains absent peripheral schizonts, cerebral malaria, and placental malaria in falciparum infection.

params.question: In leprosy, a patient at the tuberculoid pole has a strongly positive lepromin test and low bacterial index, while a patient at the lepromatous pole has a negative lepromin test and high bacterial index. What primarily determines a patient's position on this Ridley-Jopling spectrum?

answers.text: The virulence and antigenic variation of the infecting Mycobacterium leprae strain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bacterial virulence does not determine the clinical form in leprosy. The Ridley-Jopling classification is governed entirely by the strength of the host's cell-mediated immune response — the same organism produces different disease at opposite poles of the spectrum.

answers.text: The strength of the host's cell-mediated immune response

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Strong Th1 cell-mediated immunity at the tuberculoid pole forms epithelioid granulomas and clears most bacilli, yet paradoxically destroys peripheral nerves. At the lepromatous pole, T-cell anergy permits massive bacterial proliferation in foamy macrophages (lepra cells) with no granuloma formation.

answers.text: The total duration of infection before diagnosis and initiation of treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Duration of infection does not determine spectrum position. The same pathogen produces tuberculoid or lepromatous disease depending on host cell-mediated immunity — a patient with strong Th1 responses will mount granulomatous inflammation regardless of how long the infection has been present.

answers.text: The anatomical site of initial inoculation by the bacillus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The route of entry is not the determining factor. The Ridley-Jopling spectrum is governed by host cell-mediated immunity: robust Th1 responses yield tuberculoid leprosy with few bacilli, while T-cell anergy yields lepromatous leprosy with high bacterial loads.

overallFeedback.feedback: The position on the Ridley-Jopling spectrum depends on the host's cell-mediated immune response. Strong Th1 immunity → tuberculoid pole (granulomas, few bacilli, nerve damage); T-cell anergy → lepromatous pole (lepra cells, high bacterial index). Lepromin reactivity and bacterial index always move in opposite directions.
Excellent. The Ridley-Jopling spectrum is determined entirely by host cell-mediated immunity — a central paradox where strong immunity controls the bacillus but damages the nerve.

interactions.label: In Down syndrome caused by Robertsonian translocation, the recurrence risk incre

params.question: In Down syndrome caused by Robertsonian translocation, the recurrence risk increases with advancing maternal age, just as it does in free trisomy 21.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Robertsonian translocation accounts for ~4% of Down syndrome and is familial — a parent carrying the balanced translocation passes the risk regardless of age. It is free trisomy 21 (95% of cases), resulting from meiotic non-disjunction, that shows the steep increase in risk with advancing maternal age.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Robertsonian translocation (~4% of Down syndrome) fuses the long arms of chromosomes 21 and 14 and is familial: recurrence depends on whether a parent carries the balanced translocation, not on maternal age. Only free trisomy 21 (95% of cases), caused by meiotic non-disjunction, shows the well-known association with advancing maternal age.

interactions.label: A 14-month-old infant presents with bilateral leukocoria. Applying Knudson's two

params.question: A 14-month-old infant presents with bilateral leukocoria. Applying Knudson's two-hit hypothesis to the RB1 tumour suppressor gene, which mechanism best explains why hereditary retinoblastoma typically presents bilaterally?

answers.text: Both copies of the RB1 gene are deleted in the germline, so all retinal cells lack tumour suppression from birth

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complete germline loss of both RB1 alleles would likely be lethal. In hereditary retinoblastoma, only one allele carries a germline mutation. The second hit is acquired somatically — because this single hit is all that is needed per eye, bilateral disease becomes highly likely.

answers.text: A germline mutation in one RB1 allele is present in every cell, so only one additional somatic hit is needed per eye

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Knudson's two-hit hypothesis explains that hereditary retinoblastoma patients inherit a germline mutation in one RB1 allele in all cells. Only a single additional somatic mutation is needed to lose the remaining functional allele, making independent tumour development in each eye highly probable.

answers.text: The tumour in one eye metastasises to the contralateral eye via the optic chiasm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bilateral retinoblastoma arises independently in each eye, not by metastasis. The germline RB1 mutation is present in all retinal cells from birth; each eye requires only one more somatic hit to inactivate the remaining allele — this is the two-hit model.

answers.text: An environmental mutagen damages both retinae simultaneously, causing sporadic RB1 mutations in each eye

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In hereditary retinoblastoma, the first hit is a germline RB1 mutation inherited at conception — not caused by environmental exposure. The second hit occurs somatically and independently in each eye, which is why bilateral disease is the hallmark of the hereditary form.

overallFeedback.feedback: In hereditary retinoblastoma, one RB1 allele carries a germline mutation present in every cell from birth. Each eye needs only one additional somatic mutation to inactivate the remaining allele, making bilateral tumours highly likely. In sporadic cases, both hits must occur somatically in the same cell of the same eye, so the disease is unilateral and later in onset.

Well done. Knudson's two-hit hypothesis is foundational: hereditary cases carry one germline hit in every cell, so only one additional somatic hit per eye is required — explaining the bilateral, early-onset presentation.

interactions.label: Which statement correctly describes the key pathological difference between kwas

params.question: Which statement correctly describes the key pathological difference between kwashiorkor and marasmus in protein-calorie malnutrition?

answers.text: Kwashiorkor results from total calorie starvation with severe wasting; marasmus results from selective protein deficiency with oedema

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the two conditions. Kwashiorkor is caused by protein deficiency with adequate calories (producing oedema and fatty liver), while marasmus results from total calorie starvation (producing severe wasting without oedema).

answers.text: Kwashiorkor is caused by protein deficiency with adequate calories, producing low albumin, pitting oedema, and fatty liver; marasmus results from total calorie starvation with severe wasting and no oedema

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In kwashiorkor, selective protein deficiency lowers serum albumin, shifting fluid into tissues (pitting oedema) and impairing hepatic lipoprotein synthesis (fatty liver). Marasmus, from total calorie deprivation, consumes all fat and muscle stores, causing severe wasting without oedema.

answers.text: Both conditions result from total calorie deprivation but differ only in the severity of concurrent vitamin deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The fundamental distinction is caloric versus protein-selective deprivation, not vitamin status. Kwashiorkor arises from protein deficiency with relatively adequate calories, while marasmus results from total calorie starvation — these different mechanisms produce distinct clinical pictures.

answers.text: Marasmus presents with pitting oedema and hepatomegaly from fatty liver; kwashiorkor presents with muscle wasting alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the two conditions. Pitting oedema and fatty liver are hallmarks of kwashiorkor (from protein deficiency causing low albumin), not marasmus. Marasmus presents with severe wasting and loss of subcutaneous fat, without oedema.

overallFeedback.feedback: Kwashiorkor results from protein deficiency with adequate caloric intake — low serum albumin shifts fluid into tissues (pitting oedema) and impairs lipoprotein synthesis (fatty liver). Marasmus results from total calorie starvation, producing severe wasting of fat and muscle stores without oedema.

Excellent. The key distinction: kwashiorkor = protein deficiency with adequate calories → low albumin → oedema + fatty liver; marasmus = total calorie starvation → severe wasting, no oedema, no fatty liver.
